title: Sudanese gain probe into death: Long-sought Kuol inquiry welcomed
article: As the funeral for the latest victim of a shooting by a city police officer took place a few kilometres away Saturday, Calgary's Sudanese community hoped for an end to such deadly confrontations that also took one of its own in 2003.

"Police are trained to kill. This policy should change," Martin Yak, spokesman for the New Sudanese Community Association, said at a news conference announcing a fatality inquiry next summer into Deng Fermino Kuol's death.

"Why do you have to kill somebody who is committing a crime? You should arrest him so you will get to the bottom of this. But when you kill him, like they did the last person (Harjinder Singh Cheema), you won't find out why he attacked his wife and his mother- in-law. He's dead."
Yak, who speaks for the 7,500-member association on issues surrounding the Kuol death, said he is confident the probe will yield answers and bring closure.
An intoxicated Kuol, 34, died from two gunshot wounds to the neck after police responded to a disturbance at 1709 37th St. S.E. shortly after midnight on Oct. 25, 2003.
Kuol allegedly attacked Const. Ira Macumber, 41, with a knife and slashed the police officer in the arm before the officer responded in self-defence.
Kuol had come to Canada six years ago from wartorn Sudan.

The use of deadly force -- standard police policy across North America -- also came into question just weeks ago on Jan. 21, after a knife-wielding Cheema was shot by police outside of his home in Queensland moments after he'd attacked his wife and her mother. Global TV captured the shooting on camera, unleashing heated debate about the shooting for weeks after.
Sgt. Al Koenig, president of the Calgary Police Association, told the Herald Saturday the police had no option other than shooting Cheema.
Lith Akau, Kuol's cousin, agreed police need to re-examine the shoot-to-kill policy surrounding the use of deadly force.
"I want to know exactly what happened and I want the Justice Department to give out the right answers," said Akau, 41. "It was a shock when it happened . . . I'm still shocked.
"I'm glad there is an inquiry, because we don't believe (Kuol) was a violent person. We don't want to see something like this happen again. We hope the inquiry shows (police) don't have to kill."
Yak noted there may have been a problem that prompted both Cheema and Kuol to be violent and the public will never know the full story. But he welcomes the inquiry.
"I do have a great deal of confidence and respect for the Alberta judicial system," he said.
"I hope what they find will be good for the community. We hope that, after the inquiry, the community will be relieved and will have closure."

In a letter dated Jan. 24, Alberta Justice advised Yak of the inquiry, scheduled for Aug. 8-12 and Aug. 15-17. Provincial court Judge Gerald Meagher will preside and Jo-Ann Burgess will act as counsel for the justice minister and attorney general.
Doug King, chairman of justice studies at Mount Royal College, said firing a warning shot in the air or aiming at a limb to disable a charging armed assailant is "too risky."

RCMP Sgt. Gilles Deziel, a former defensive tactics instructor and firearms expert based in Ottawa, said an officer must act if he fears for his or somebody else's life and must prevent being stabbed.
Yak said there has been frustration with the lengthy delay, but Alberta Justice spokeswoman Shannon Haggarty said it just takes time.
"We have said earlier a full public inquiry would take place," said Haggarty. "It's automatic and mandatory when a police officer is involved."

The Calgary police homicide unit initially investigated the shooting, according to service policy, then turned its findings over for review to the department's professional standards section and an Edmonton special Crown prosecutor.
They subsequently cleared Macumber, a four-year member of the police force, of any wrongdoing.
A judge hearing a fatality inquiry can make recommendations to prevent similar incidents, but they are not binding.
